claims.claim: A central assumption about heritable genomic markers is that they are generated by two homogeneous Poisson mutation processes along the genome and through time.
claims.source: A central assumption about heritable genomic markers is that they are generated by two homogeneous Poisson mutation processes along the genome as well as through time.
claims.evidence: This is a fundamental modeling assumption in coalescent theory.

claims.claim: Mutations in different genealogies are independent due to the effect of recombination.
claims.source: This entails that mutations in different genealogies are independent due to the effect of recombination (Wiuf and Hein, 1999; McVean and Cardin, 2005), and that there are no time periods with a large excess, or a severe lack, of mutations along a genealogy (mutations are independently distributed in time within a DNA fragment).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on recombination and mutation.

claims.claim: Model violations such as variation in recombination and mutation rates along the genome can compromise the accuracy of demographic and selective inference.
claims.source: Despite the power of the SMC, well-known model violations such as variation in recombination and mutation rates along the genome (Barroso et al., 2019; Barroso and Dutheil, 2023) or pervasive selection (Schraiber and Akey, 2015; Johri et al., 2021; Johri et al., 2020) can compromise the accuracy of demographic and selective inference (Gattepaille et al., 2013; Sellinger et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting these issues.

claims.claim: Inferences can be biased when the population recombination rate (ρ) is higher than the population mutation rate (θ).
claims.source: The first issue occurs when the population recombination rate (ρ) is higher than the population mutation rate (θ). In such cases, inferences can be biased if not erroneous (Terhorst et al., 2017; Sellinger et al., 2021; Sellinger et al., 2020), because several recombination events cannot be inferred due to the lack of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs for point mutations).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this bias.

claims.claim: The typical low mutation rate of 10^-9 up to 10^-8 per base per generation places strong limitations on SMC analysis of recent bottleneck events.
claims.source: The typical low mutation rate of 10−9 up to 10−8 (per base, per generation) found in most species, therefore, places strong limitations on SMC analysis of recent bottleneck events (up to ca. 104 generations ago) when inference is based solely on SNP data.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between mutation rates and temporal resolution.

claims.claim: Bottlenecks are often either not found, or when inferred, their timing and magnitude are not well estimated.
claims.source: Indeed, bottlenecks are often either not found, or when inferred, their timing and magnitude are not well estimated (inferred smoother than in reality, Johri et al., 2021; Sellinger et al., 2021), even when a large number of samples is used.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting these limitations.

claims.claim: Current SMC, DL, or ABC inference methods rely almost exclusively on SNPs for inference.
claims.source: Nonetheless, current SMC, DL, or ABC inference methods making use of full genome sequence data rely almost exclusively on SNPs for inference (Schiffels and Durbin, 2014; Terhorst et al., 2017; Sellinger et al., 2020; Boitard et al., 2016; Korfmann et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to major inference methods.

claims.claim: SNPs are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data.
claims.source: There are both practical and theoretical reasons for using SNPs: They are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data and their mutational process is well approximated by the infinite site model (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008), simplifying the inference of the underlying genealogy.
claims.evidence: This is a known practical advantage of SNPs in genomic studies.

claims.claim: The mutational process of SNPs is well approximated by the infinite site model.
claims.source: There are both practical and theoretical reasons for using SNPs: They are easily detectable from short-read re-sequencing data and their mutational process is well approximated by the infinite site model (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010; Wakeley, 2008), simplifying the inference of the underlying genealogy.
claims.evidence: This is a standard theoretical assumption supported by citations.

claims.claim: Other heritable genomic markers exist whose mutation rates can be several orders of magnitude higher than that of SNPs.
claims.source: However, other heritable genomic markers exist whose mutation rates can be several orders of magnitude higher than that of SNPs and could thus be more informative about recent demographic events.
claims.evidence: This is supported by known mutation rates of microsatellites, TEs, and methylation sites.

claims.claim: Current technological limitations impede the easy detection and estimation of allele frequencies for many heritable markers.
claims.source: Current technological limitations still impede the easy detection and estimation of allele frequencies for many of these markers (Yang et al., 2018; Ou et al., 2019; Wang, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on marker detection challenges.

claims.claim: Identifying insertion/excision variation of transposable elements or copy number variation of microsatellites requires a high-quality reference genome and ideally long-read sequencing approaches.
claims.source: For example, identifying insertion/excision variation of transposable elements or copy number variation of microsatellites requires a high-quality reference genome and ideally long-read sequencing approaches (Ou et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on TE detection methods.

claims.claim: DNA cytosine methylation is emerging as a potentially useful epigenetic marker for phylogenetic inference in plants.
claims.source: In addition to these genomic markers, DNA cytosine methylation is emerging as a potentially useful epigenetic marker for phylogenetic inference in plants (Yao et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on methylation-based phylogenetics.

claims.claim: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides arise at a rate of ca. 10^-4 up to 10^-3 per site per generation.
claims.source: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides, in particular, arise at a rate of ca. 10−4 up to 10−3 per site per generation (that is 4–5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations, van der Graaf et al., 2015), and can be inherited across generations (Pisupati et al., 2023; Weigel and Colot, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies measuring epimutation rates.

claims.claim: CG methylation changes occur 4-5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations.
claims.source: Stochastic gains and losses of DNA methylation at CG dinucleotides, in particular, arise at a rate of ca. 10−4 up to 10−3 per site per generation (that is 4–5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA point mutations, van der Graaf et al., 2015), and can be inherited across generations (Pisupati et al., 2023; Weigel and Colot, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the cited epimutation and mutation rates.

claims.claim: Spontaneous epimutations are likely neutral at the genome-wide scale.
claims.source: These so-called spontaneous epimutations are likely neutral at the genome-wide scale (Vidalis et al., 2016; Johannes and Schmitz, 2019b, but see Muyle et al., 2021; Pisupati et al., 2023), and can be easily detected from bisulphite converted short read sequencing data (Lister et al., 2008; Schmitz et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on epimutation neutrality, with caveats noted.

claims.claim: CG methylation data can be used as a molecular clock for timing divergence between pairs of lineages over timescales ranging from years to decades.
claims.source: Recent work suggests that CG methylation data can be used as a molecular clock for timing divergence between pairs of lineages over timescales ranging from years to decades (Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study demonstrating this application.

claims.claim: The mutational process at hyper-mutable markers is reversible and more consistent with a finite site model.
claims.source: Because of the high mutation rate, the mutational process at these (hyper-mutable) markers is reversible and more consistent with a finite site, rather than infinite site, model, which can result in extensive homoplasy (as known for microsatellite markers, Estoup et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical inference supported by a citation to work on microsatellites.

claims.claim: Classic expectations of population genetics diversity statistics need to be revised for hyper-mutable markers.
claims.source: Indeed, classic expectations of population genetics diversity statistics, mostly built for SNPs, need to be revised for these hyper-mutable markers (Charlesworth and Jain, 2014; Wang and Fan, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on hyper-mutable markers.

claims.claim: With the inclusion of hyper-mutable marker 2, SMCtheo correctly infers the rapid change of population size of the bottleneck.
claims.source: However, with the inclusion of hyper-mutable marker 2, our SMCtheo approach correctly infers the rapid change of population size of the bottleneck (Figure 2A, green).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where the green line accurately captures the bottleneck.

claims.claim: Accurate estimation of demography is obtained even when the mutation rate of marker 2 is unknown.
claims.source: It is encouraging that an accurate estimation of the demography is obtained, even when the mutation rate of marker 2 is unknown (Figure 2A, blue).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A where the blue line shows good demographic inference.

claims.claim: In the absence of hyper-mutable marker 2, no approach can correctly infer variation of population size when the effective population size is small (N=1,000).
claims.source: We find that in the absence of the hyper-mutable marker 2, no approach can correctly infer the variation of population size.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B where methods using only marker 1 fail to detect the bottleneck.

claims.claim: When integrating both markers, population size can be recovered even if the mutation rate of marker 2 is not a priori known.
claims.source: Yet, when integrating both markers, the population size can be recovered, even if the mutation rate of marker 2 is not a priori known.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B where both green and blue lines recover the bottleneck.

claims.claim: A very small proportion (0.1%) of hyper-mutable genomic sites is sufficient to significantly improve the accuracy of inferences.
claims.source: This suggests that a very small proportion of hyper-mutable genomic sites is sufficient to significantly improve the accuracy of inferences.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing improved inference with only 0.1% marker 2 sites.

claims.claim: By integrating genomic marker 2 which mutation rate is larger than the recombination rate, estimates of the recombination rate and past population size variation are substantially improved.
claims.source: Our results show that by integrating the genomic marker 2 which mutation rate is larger than the recombination rate, estimates of the recombination rate as well as past population size variation are substantially improved (Table 2, Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Table 2 and Figure 2C showing improved parameter estimates.

claims.claim: The true recombination rate can be recovered well even with marker 1 only by directly optimizing the likelihood.
claims.source: However, by directly optimizing the likelihood, the true recombination rate can be recovered well even with marker 1 only.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Table 2 where the LH method with 1 marker estimates 0.84×10^-7 compared to the true value of 10^-7.

claims.claim: SMCm can accurately recover site- and region-level epimutation rates except when these are higher than 10^-4.
claims.source: Our SMCm approach can accurately recover these rates except when these are higher than 10-4.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Supplementary file 1c and d showing estimation accuracy.

claims.claim: When epimutation rates are very high (close to 10^-2), accuracy is lost compared to slower epimutation rates.
claims.source: Similar to our previous observation, we find that when the epimutation rates are very high (e.g. close to 10-2), accuracy is lost compared to slower epimutation rates.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Average estimated epimutation rates are off from the true value by less than a factor of 10 when rates are very high.
claims.source: Nonetheless, our average estimated rates are off from the true value by less than a factor 10.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the results in Supplementary file 1e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate.
claims.source: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate (Figure 4C), while the LD between SNPs can range over few kbp (Figure 4D, as observed in A. thaliana [Cao et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013]).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C showing rapid LD decay for epimutations.

claims.claim: The LD between SNPs can range over few kbp in A. thaliana.
claims.source: There is virtually no linkage disequilibrium (LD) between epimutations due to the high epimutation rate (Figure 4C), while the LD between SNPs can range over few kbp (Figure 4D, as observed in A. thaliana [Cao et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013]).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and supported by citations to A. thaliana studies.

claims.claim: The simulator generates SNPs, SMPs, and DMRs which fulfill the three key assumptions from Figure 1A.
claims.source: In other words, our simulator generates SNPs, SMPs, and DMRs, which fulfil the three key assumptions from Figure 1A.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the LD and distribution analyses in Figure 4.

claims.claim: When the site epimutation rates are a priori known, the sharp decrease of population size can be accurately detected.
claims.source: When the site epimutation rates are a priori known, the sharp decrease of population size can be accurately detected.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B where the demographic inference accurately captures the bottleneck.

claims.claim: When epimutation rates are unknown, the shape of past demographic history is well inferred except for a scaling issue.
claims.source: When epimutation rates are unknown, the shape of the past demographic history is also well inferred except for a scaling issue (a shift along the x- and y-axes similar to that in Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing good shape recovery with some scaling differences.

claims.claim: Having methylation measurements for as low as 2% of all CG sites is sufficient to improve SNP-based demographic inference.
claims.source: This suggests that having methylation measurements for as low as 2% of all CG sites being epimutable in the genome is entirely sufficient to improved SNP-based demographic inference (eSMC2 in Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and B where 2%, 10%, and 20% methylation sites yield similar improvements.

claims.claim: Incorporating SMPs with known site-level epimutations leads to substantial inference improvements when sequence length is reduced to 10 Mb.
claims.source: However, incorporating SMPs with known site-level epimutations into the model leads to substantial inference improvements (Figure 5C, D, Supplementary file 1f).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D where SMCm outperforms eSMC2 with limited data.

claims.claim: Integrating epimutations slightly improves the accuracy of TMRCA when the epimutation rates are known.
claims.source: We confirm our intuition that integrating epimutations slightly improves the accuracy of TMRCA when the epimutation rates are known but does not when the rates are unknown.
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Supplementary file 1g showing RMSE values for TMRCA inference.

claims.claim: A gain of accuracy is observed when integrating DMR data with known epimutation rates.
claims.source: As in Figure 5, we observed a gain of accuracy in inference when region-level epimutation rates are known, while the length of the region (1 kb or 150 bp) does not seem to affect the result.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No significant gain of information is observed when integrating DMR data with unknown epimutation rates.
claims.source: However, no significant gain of information is observed when integrating DMR data with unknown epimutation rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2 where unknown rates don't improve inference.

claims.claim: CG methylation SMPs and to a lesser extent DMRs can be used jointly with SNPs to improve demographic inference, especially in recent times.
claims.source: In summary, CG methylation SMPs and to a lesser extend DMRs, can be used jointly with SNPs to improve demographic inference (Supplementary file 1h presents the corresponding RMSE values for demographic inference shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), especially in recent times (Supplementary file 1f and h).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple simulation results and RMSE calculations.

claims.claim: When epimutation rates are unknown, there is a gain of accuracy when integrating epimutations, especially in recent times.
claims.source: When the epimutations rates are unknown, we observe a gain of accuracy when integrating epimutations, especially in recent times.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for simulations with both site and region epimutations.

claims.claim: When epimutation rates are a priori known, there is a loss of accuracy when accounting for epimutations in the presence of both site and region processes.
claims.source: However, when epimutation rates are a priori known, we observe a loss of accuracy when accounting for epimutations.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and explained by mislabeling of methylation region status.

claims.claim: The loss of accuracy when epimutation rates are known is due to mislabeling of the methylation region status when site and region-level epimutations occur jointly at similar rates.
claims.source: This loss of accuracy is due to the mislabeling of the methylation region status (in step 1) when site and region-level epimutations occur jointly at similar rates (as there will be methylated sites in unmethylated regions and unmethylated sites in methylated regions).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of the algorithm and the observed results.

claims.claim: Ignoring site or region-level processes can decrease the accuracy of inference.
claims.source: We show that (1) using SMPs we can unveil past demographic events hidden by limitations in SNPs, (2) the correct demography can be uncovered irrespective of knowing a priori the epimutation rates, (3) ignoring site or region-level processes can decrease the accuracy of inference, and (4) knowing the epimutation rates may improve the estimate of demography compared to simultaneously estimating them with SMCm.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing decreased accuracy when region effects are ignored.

claims.claim: For all 10 individual A. thaliana methylomes, the hypothesis of a binomial distribution of methylated and unmethylated sites along the genomes is rejected.
claims.source: As expected from Denkena et al., 2021, for all 10 individual full methylomes, we reject the hypothesis of a binomial distribution of methylated and unmethylated sites along the genomes, suggesting the existence of region effect methylation (yielding DMRs), meaning that CG are more likely to be methylated if in a highly methylated region, and conversely for unmethylated CG.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result from the A. thaliana data analysis.

claims.claim: The average p-value is smaller than 0.05 for distances up to 2,000 bp between CG methylation sites in A. thaliana.
claims.source: We observe an average p-value smaller than 0.05 for distances up to 2,000 bp but then the p-value rapidly increases (>0.4) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5 plotting p-values against distance.

claims.claim: The HMM yields a DMR average length of 222 bp in A. thaliana.
claims.source: As a second measure, our HMM (based on pairs of genomes) yields a DMR average length of 222 bp (distribution in Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the A. thaliana data and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The minimum distance for epimutations to be independent along a genome is over 2 kb in A. thaliana.
claims.source: We conclude that the minimum distance for epimutations to be independent along a genome is over 2 kb and spans larger distances than the typically proposed DMR size (ca. 150 bp in Denkena et al., 2021 and 222 bp in our analysis) and can therefore cover the size of a gene (see Muyle et al., 2021; Briffa et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the p-value analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The epimutation processes that produce DMRs at the population level in plants cannot simply result from the cumulative action of single-site epimutations.
claims.source: The simulations and data from A. thaliana indicates that the epimutation processes that produce DMRs at the population level in plants cannot simply result from the cumulative action of single-site epimutations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing simulations with only site-level epimutations to observed data patterns.

claims.claim: The autocorrelation in CG methylation is a function of cooperative methylation maintenance and the distribution of histone modifications.
claims.source: This insight is consistent with recent analyses of epimutational processes in gene bodies, which seems to indicate that the autocorrelation in CG methylation is a function of cooperative methylation maintenance and the distribution of histone modifications (Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent mechanistic studies.

claims.claim: DMRs are, on average, twice as large as the inferred genomic genealogy span in A. thaliana: average length of 222 bp (DMR) vs 137 bp (genealogy).
claims.source: We observe that both distributions have a similar shape, but DMRs are, on average, twice as large as the inferred genomic genealogy span: average length of 222 bp (DMR) vs 137 bp (genealogy) and median length of 134 bp (DMR) vs 62 bp (genealogy).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the distributions shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: On average, DMRs are larger than the average distance between two recombination events in A. thaliana, violating the homogeneous distribution of epimutations along the genome.
claims.source: This means that, on average, DMRs are larger than the average distance between two recombination events, thus violating the homogeneous distribution of epimutations along the genome (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of DMR and genealogy span distributions in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The LD between SMPs in A. thaliana data is high for distances smaller than 100 bp.
claims.source: We find the LD between SMPs in the data to be high (and higher than LD between SNPs) for distances smaller than 100 bp (red line in Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C comparing LD decay between data and simulations.

claims.claim: The LD decay of SMPs is much faster than for SNPs in A. thaliana.
claims.source: The LD decay of SMPs is much faster than for SNPs (no linkage disequilibrium between epimutations for distances >100 bp), likely stemming from (1) epimutation rates being much higher than the DNA mutation rate, and (2) the high per-site recombination rate in A. thaliana.
claims.evidence: This is observed in Figure 4C and D and explained by known rate differences.

claims.claim: The LD between SMPs at distances smaller than 100 bp in A. thaliana is much higher compared to simulations.
claims.source: Moreover, the LD between SMPs at distances smaller than 100 bp in A. thaliana being much higher compared to our simulations (Figure 4C), we suggest that additional local mechanisms of epimutation processes may not be accounted for in our model of the region-level methylation process.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing red and blue lines in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When using SNP data only, the demographic results for A. thaliana are similar to those previously found, with no strong evidence for an expansion post-Last Glacial Maximum.
claims.source: When using SNP data only, the demographic results are similar to those previously found (Sellinger et al., 2020; Strütt et al., 2023; Figure 6 purple lines), with no strong evidence for an expansion post-Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) (Cao et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (purple lines) and supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: When using empirically inferred methylation and demethylation rates, a mild bottleneck post-LGM is followed by recent expansion in A. thaliana.
claims.source: When we use as input the methylation and demethylation rates that have been inferred experimentally (van der Graaf et al., 2015), a mild bottleneck post-LGM is followed by recent expansion (Figure 6 blue lines).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (blue lines) using fixed epimutation rates.

claims.claim: When SMCm estimates the epimutation rates, a strong bottleneck event occurs between ca. 5,000 and 10,000 generations ago in A. thaliana, followed by an expansion until today.
claims.source: By contrast, letting our SMCm estimate the epimutation rates, we find in recent times a somehow similar but stronger demographic change post-LGM. We find a strong bottleneck event occurring between ca. 5,000 and 10,000 generations ago, followed by an expansion until today (Figure 6 green lines).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 (green lines) when epimutation rates are estimated.

claims.claim: The inferred site epimutation rates in A. thaliana are 10,000 times faster than the DNA mutation rate.
claims.source: The inferred site epimutation rates are 10,000 faster than the DNA mutation rate (Supplementary file 1k), which is close to the expected order of magnitude from experimental measures with and without DMR effects (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the inferred rates in Supplementary file 1k and compared to experimental measures.

claims.claim: The inclusion of DNA methylation data can aid in the accurate reconstruction of the evolutionary history of populations, particularly in the recent past.
claims.source: These results indicate that the inclusion of DNA methylation data can aid in the accurate reconstruction of the evolutionary history of populations, particularly in the recent past, where SNPs reach their resolution limit.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the A. thaliana analysis results in Figure 6.

claims.claim: DNA methylation status at CG dinucleotides undergoes stochastic changes at rates several orders of magnitude higher than the DNA mutation rate and can be inherited across generations.
claims.source: This is made possible by the fact that the DNA methylation status at CG dinucleotide undergoes stochastic changes at rates that are several orders of magnitude higher than the DNA mutation rate and can be inherited across generations similar to DNA mutations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies on epimutation rates and heritability.

claims.claim: By integrating multiple heritable genomic markers, population size variation in very recent time can be more accurately recovered.
claims.source: We demonstrate that by integrating multiple heritable genomic markers, the population size variation in very recent time can be more accurately recovered (outperforming any other methods given the amount of data used in this study [Terhorst et al., 2017; Speidel et al., 2019]).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the Results section with various simulation scenarios.

claims.claim: Correctly integrating multiple genomic markers can improve TMRCA inference.
claims.source: Our results indicate that correctly integrating multiple genomic marker can improve TRMCA inference, which is becoming a field of high interest (Korfmann et al., 2024; Hubisz et al., 2020; Mahmoudi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RMSE calculations in Supplementary file 1g and citations to relevant work.

claims.claim: If the SNP mutation rate is known, the mutation rate of other markers can be recovered under the condition that the marker follows all hypotheses described in Figure 1.
claims.source: Our simulations demonstrate that if the SNP mutation rate is known, the mutation rate of other markers can be recovered (under the condition that the marker follow all hypotheses described in Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Table 1 showing accurate mutation rate estimation.

claims.claim: The method accounts for the finite site problem that arises at reversible (hyper-mutable) markers and/or where effective population size is high.
claims.source: Moreover, our method accounts for the finite site problem that arises at reversible (hyper-mutable) markers and/or where effective population size is high (Tellier et al., 2011; Upadhya and Steinrücken, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a design feature of the method supported by citations to relevant theoretical work.

claims.claim: Comparisons of LD for different markers along the genome is a useful way to assess violations of model assumptions.
claims.source: We find that comparisons of LD for different markers along the genome is a useful way to assess violations of our model assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C and D where LD patterns reveal model violations.

claims.claim: A. thaliana presents the largest genetic and epigenetic data-set of high quality.
claims.source: Indeed, A. thaliana presents the largest genetic and epigenetic data-set of high quality.
claims.evidence: This is a known fact about A. thaliana as a model organism.

claims.claim: The methylation state in CG context in A. thaliana is mainly heritable and well documented.
claims.source: Additionally, the methylation states in CG context has been proven mainly heritable and is well documented (Denkena et al., 2021; Hazarika et al., 2022; van der Graaf et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies on CG methylation heritability.

claims.claim: The model-based approach provides strong evidence that DMRs cannot simply emerge from spontaneous site-level epimutations that arise according to Poisson processes along the genome.
claims.source: Our model-based approach provides strong evidence that DMRs cannot simply emerge from spontaneous site-level epimutations that arise according to a Poisson processes along genome.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing model predictions to observed data patterns.

claims.claim: Stochastic changes in region-level methylation states must be the outcome of spontaneous methylation and demethylation events that operate at both the site- and region-level.
claims.source: Instead, stochastic changes in region-level methylation states must be the outcome of spontaneous methylation and demethylation events that operate at both the site- and region-level (as corroborated by Pisupati et al., 2023; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis and supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: The epimutation model cannot fully describe the observed diversity of epimutations along the genome.
claims.source: Our epimutation model cannot fully describe the observed diversity of epimutations along the genome (Denkena et al., 2021), meaning that the epimutation processes may indeed be more complex than expected (Denkena et al., 2021; Hazarika et al., 2022; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from discrepancies between model predictions and observed data.

claims.claim: Non-independence is observed between annotated methylation sites spanning genomic regions larger than the span of the underlying genealogy in A. thaliana.
claims.source: We observe non-independence between annotated methylation sites spanning genomic regions larger than the span of the underlying genealogy (determined by recombination events) which no model can currently describe.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the p-value analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Methylation probably violates the assumptions of a Poisson process distribution along the genome and in time.
claims.source: Thus, methylation probably violate the assumptions of a Poisson process distribution along the genome and in time (i.e. Figure 1), in line with recent functional studies (Pisupati et al., 2023; Hazarika et al., 2022; Lyons et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from observed LD patterns and supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: Caution is warranted against conclusions on the role of natural selection based on population epigenomic data due to violation of model assumptions.
claims.source: We thus further caution against conclusions on the role of natural (purifying) selection (Muyle et al., 2021) or its absence (Vidalis et al., 2016) based on population epigenomic data due to the violation of the above-mentioned assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on the observed model violations.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between inferred and experimentally measured epimutation rates is suspected to be due to model violations.
claims.source: Additionally, we suspect those model violations to explain the discrepancy between the epimutation rates we inferred and the ones measured experimentally (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed discrepancies.

claims.claim: An Ising model is suggested as a possible way forward for modeling epimutations to account for heterogeneous methylation processes.
claims.source: We thus suggest a possible way forward for modeling epimutations through an Ising model (Zhang et al., 2018) to account for the heterogeneous methylation process.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future methodological development.

claims.evidence: This is based on preliminary analyses and cited simulation results.

claims.claim: There is a need to develop a more realistic methylation model for epimutations.
claims.source: Hence, there is a need to develop a more realistic methylation model for epimutations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed limitations of current models.

claims.claim: The distance of LD decay for SMPs matches quite well the estimated distance between recombination events.
claims.source: Interestingly, the distance of LD decay for SMPs matches quite well the estimated distance between recombination events (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing LD decay patterns to recombination event spacing in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A restricted focus on segregating SMPs in genic regions could meet model assumptions reasonably well.
claims.source: Nonetheless, we find that a restricted focus on segregating SMPs in genic regions could meet our model assumptions reasonably well, and thus provides a promising way forward.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the better fit of SMPs compared to DMRs to model assumptions.

claims.claim: Using segregating SMPs, a past demographic bottleneck followed by an expansion is recovered which could fit the post-Last Glacial Maximum colonization of Europe.
claims.source: Using these segregating SMPs, we recover a past demographic bottleneck followed by an expansion which could fit the post- Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) colonization of Europe (although caution must be taken concerning the reliability of those results as pointed above), a hypothesized scenario (François et al., 2008) which could not be clearly identified using SNPs only from European (relic and non-relic) accessions (Cao et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and compared to previous SNP-only studies.

claims.claim: Current results for A. thaliana demography are limited by theoretical frameworks unable to simultaneously account for extensive background selection, population structure, and variation in molecular rates.
claims.source: Indeed, beyond the limits of using SNPs only, current results are limited by theoretical frameworks unable to simultaneously account (and disentangle) for extensive background selection (reinforced by very high selfing), population structure and variation in molecular rates (e.g. mutation rates, Monroe et al., 2022), which are all known to be present in A. thaliana.
claims.evidence: This is a known limitation in the field supported by citations.

claims.source: We also note that using CG methylated sites in genic regions may be problematic as the typical genealogies at these loci could be shorter than the genome average due to the presence of background selection, thus making the inference of such short TMRCA more difficult (even with SMPs) than in non-coding regions (which do not harbour desirable CG methylation sites, van der Graaf et al., 2015; Vidalis et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known effects of background selection and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Simultaneously accounting for multiple heritable markers can help disentangle different evolutionary forces, such as between selection and variation in mutation rate.
claims.source: We suggest that simultaneously accounting for multiple heritable markers can help disentangle different evolutionary forces, such as between selection and variation in mutation rate: selection has a local effect on the population genealogy, while the mutation rate variation would only locally affect that given marker but not the genealogy (Charlesworth and Jensen, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical suggestion supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The absence of conflicting demography inferred from SNPs and from methylation confirms that at the time scale of thousands of generations, CG methylation sites are mainly heritable.
claims.source: The absence of conflicting demography inferred from SNPs and from methylation confirms at the time scale of thousands of generations, CG methylation sites are mainly heritable and can be modeled using population genetics theory (Charlesworth and Jain, 2014; Vidalis et al., 2016 but see Pisupati et al., 2023) and used to estimate divergence between lineages (Yao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of demographic estimates and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Fast ecological local adaptation and response to stresses may likely not be prominent forces endlessly reshaping CG methylation patterns.
claims.source: In other words, fast ecological local adaptation (Schmid et al., 2018) and response to stresses (Srikant and Drost, 2020) may likely not be prominent forces endlessly reshaping CG methylation patterns (non-heritability in Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of demographic estimates and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The approach provides inference tools to study markers' rates and distribution process along the genome without requiring additional experimental data when evolutionary mechanisms are not well understood.
claims.source: If the epimutations/genomic markers evolutionary mechanisms are not well understood (Pisupati et al., 2023; Briffa et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2023), our approach provides inference tools to study the markers' rates and distribution process along the genome, without requiring additional experimental data.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ability to estimate mutation rates shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: When the evolution of epimutations/genomic markers is well understood and can be modeled, these can be integrated to improve SMC performance.
claims.source: If the evolution of epimutations/genomic markers are well understood (including a measure of the mutation rates) and can be modeled to describe the observed intra-population diversity, these can be integrated to improve the SMC performance.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B and D where known rates improve inference.

claims.claim: When applying the approach to genome-wide genetic and epigenetic data, it is advisable to use accurately annotated markers with information regarding their inheritance and mutational properties.
claims.source: Hence, when applying our approach to genome-wide genetic and epigenetic data, it is advisable to use accurately annotated markers with, if possible, information regarding their inheritance and mutational properties.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed importance of accurate marker characterization.

claims.claim: The set of gene body methylated genes are likely the optimal choice for methylation analysis.
claims.source: Regarding methylation specifically, while the set of gene body methylated genes previously used (Vidalis et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2023) are likely the optimal choice (Yao et al., 2021), these are too few and too scattered across the genome to maximize the statistical power of SMC methods.
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies and practical considerations.

claims.claim: Despite the wealth of functional studies and data on methylation in A. thaliana, the distribution of epimutations is not fully understood.
claims.source: Yet, despite the wealth of functional studies and data on methylation in A. thaliana, the distribution of epimutations is not fully understood (Hazarika et al., 2022; Pisupati et al., 2023), but independent rates for sites and region-level have been estimated (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Denkena et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies highlighting knowledge gaps.

claims.claim: When accounting for region-level epimutations, the algorithm requires first inferring the methylation status of a region via an HMM to later compute epimutation probabilities.
claims.source: When accounting for region-level epimutations, our algorithm requires first inferring via an HMM the methylation status of a region in order to later on compute the epimutation probabilities (i.e. the emission matrix of the SMC HMM).
claims.evidence: This describes the algorithmic approach used in the method.

claims.claim: In the presence of site and region-level epimutations occurring at similar rates, recovering the region methylation status becomes harder.
claims.source: Hence, in the presence of site and region-level epimutations occurring at similar rates, recovering the region methylation status becomes harder as methylated sites are observed in the unmethylated regions (and unmethylated sites observed in the methylated regions).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the algorithmic challenge based on the nature of the data.

claims.claim: Mislabeling of the region methylation status leads to accuracy loss due to the use of wrong emission probability at later steps of SMC inference.
claims.source: The mislabelling of the region methylation status lead to accuracy loss due to the use of the wrong emission probability at the later steps of the SMC inference (Forward-Backward algorithm).
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism of accuracy loss observed in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: When epimutation rates are freely inferred, their values are based on the estimated methylation region status and are sufficiently consistent to contain information and slightly improve inference accuracy.
claims.source: When epimutation rates are freely inferred, their values are based on the estimated methylation region status. Therefore, even if the inferred rates are incorrect, these are sufficiently consistent with the inferred region methylation status to contain information and slightly improve inference accuracy.
claims.evidence: This explains the results in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 where unknown rates still improve inference.

claims.claim: Extra care must be taken when dealing with epigenomic data in other species due to potential differences of methylation between different tissues or pools of cells.
claims.source: Additionally, extra care must be taken when dealing with epigenomic data in other species as the SMP calling might not be as simple as for Arabidopsis thaliana due to potential difference of methylation between different tissues or pool of cells.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary note based on known biological variation in methylation.

claims.claim: The potential dependence between SNPs and SMPs is ignored in the current analysis.
claims.source: Similarly, we ignore here the potential dependence between SNPs and SMPs, as more empirical evidence (and modeling) is required to quantify the potential interaction between both mutational processes.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit statement of a modeling assumption.

claims.claim: With new sequencing technology, long and accurate reads are becoming accessible, leading to high-quality reference genomes for model and non-model species.
claims.source: On a brighter note, with the release of new sequencing technology (Lang et al., 2020), long and accurate reads are becoming accessible, leading to the availability of highquality reference genomes for model and non-model species alike (Nurk et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent technological advances.

claims.claim: The quality of re-sequencing genome data and their annotations is enhanced so that additional markers can be called with increasing confidence.
claims.source: Additionally, the quality of re-sequencing (population sample) genome data and their annotations is enhanced so that additional markers such as transposable elements, insertion, deletion or microsatellites can be called with increasing confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about ongoing technological improvements in the field.

claims.claim: In the near future, there will be an improvement in understanding of the heritability of many markers besides SNPs.
claims.source: We therefore suspect that, in the near future, there will be an improvement in our understanding of the heritability of many markers besides SNPs.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future research developments.

claims.claim: Adding other genomic markers besides SNPs will improve full genome approaches, which are currently limited by observed nucleotide diversity.
claims.source: Adding other genomic markers besides SNPs will improve full genome approaches, which are currently limited by the observed nucleotide diversity (Kelleher et al., 2019; Speidel et al., 2019; Schweiger and Durbin, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on current limitations and the results of this study.

claims.source: Additionally, the potential complexity resulting by integrating multiple independent markers could be tackled by the use of continuous time Markov chains for the emission matrix.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for methodological improvement.

claims.claim: The results pave the way to improve inference of biological traits or recombination rate through time.
claims.source: We predict that our results pave the way to improve the inference of (1) biological traits or recombination rate through time (Deng et al., 2021; Strütt et al., 2023), (2) multiple merger events (Korfmann et al., 2024), and (3) recombination and mutation rate maps (Barroso et al., 2019; Barroso and Dutheil, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future applications supported by citations.

claims.claim: The method should help dissect the effect of evolutionary forces on genomic diversity.
claims.source: Our method also should help to dissect the effect of evolutionary forces on genomic diversity (Johri et al., 2022; Johri et al., 2021), and to improve the simultaneous detection, quantification and dating of selection events (Albers and McVean, 2020; Bisschop et al., 2021; Johri et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future applications supported by citations.

claims.claim: Extending this work by simultaneously integrating diverse types of genomic markers into other theoretical frameworks likely represents the future of population genomics.
claims.source: Hence, there is no doubt that extending our work, by simultaneously integrating diverse types of genomic markers into other theoretical framework (e.g. ABC approaches), likely represents the future of population genomics, especially to study species for which many thousands of samples cannot be obtained.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future direction of the field.

claims.claim: The approach helps develop more general classes of models capable of leveraging information from any type and amount of diversity observed in sequencing data.
claims.source: We believe our approach helps to develop more general classes of models capable of leveraging information from any type and amount of diversity observed in sequencing data, and thus to challenge our current understanding of genome evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the broader impact of the methodological framework.

results.result: The extended SMC framework (SMCtheo) that integrates hyper-mutable markers with SNPs improves demographic inference accuracy in recent times and can uncover bottleneck events that SNP-only methods fail to detect. This improvement is achieved even when the mutation rate of the hyper-mutable marker is unknown, and requires only a very small proportion (0.1-2%) of hyper-mutable sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide simulation evidence from Figure 2 showing that SMCtheo accurately recovers recent bottlenecks when hyper-mutable markers are included, while SNP-only methods (MSMC2, eSMC2) fail. The results hold across different population sizes (N=10,000 and N=1,000) and with minimal proportions of hyper-mutable sites. Table 2 and Figure 2C demonstrate improved recombination rate estimates when marker 2 mutation rate exceeds recombination rate.

results.result: The SMCtheo framework can accurately infer mutation rates of hyper-mutable markers under a finite site model when the SNP mutation rate is known, provided the marker follows the model assumptions in Figure 1.
results.evaluation: Table 1 demonstrates accurate estimation of marker 2 mutation rates across a range from 10^-8 to 10^-4, with coefficients of variation below 0.05. However, accuracy degrades at very high rates (10^-2), where estimates are off by approximately a factor of 3. The condition that markers must follow Figure 1 assumptions is clearly stated.

results.result: Segregating single methylated polymorphisms (SMPs) satisfy the SMC modeling assumptions with virtually no linkage disequilibrium beyond 100 bp due to high epimutation rates, and the LD decay distance matches well with the estimated distance between recombination events.
results.evaluation: Figure 4C and 4D demonstrate rapid LD decay for SMPs compared to SNPs in both simulations and A. thaliana data. The simulator generates SNPs, SMPs, and DMRs that fulfill the three key assumptions from Figure 1A (C58). The LD decay pattern for SMPs aligns with recombination event spacing (C105), supporting the suitability of SMPs for SMC analysis.

results.result: Differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are not suitable for SMC analysis because their average length (222 bp) is approximately twice as large as the genomic distance between recombination events (137 bp), violating the assumption of homogeneous distribution of epimutations along the genome.
results.evaluation: Figure 4B provides direct quantitative evidence comparing DMR lengths to genealogy spans in A. thaliana, showing DMRs average 222 bp versus 137 bp for genealogies (median 134 bp vs 62 bp). This size discrepancy means DMRs span multiple genealogies, violating the spatial homogeneity assumption illustrated in Figure 1C.

results.result: The SMCm method can accurately recover site- and region-level epimutation rates except when rates exceed 10^-4, though even at very high rates (close to 10^-2) the estimates are within a factor of 10 of true values.
results.evaluation: Supplementary file 1c, d, and e along with Figure 4—figure supplement 1 demonstrate the accuracy of epimutation rate estimation across different rate values. The accuracy limitation at high rates is clearly documented, but the method maintains reasonable performance even under challenging conditions.

results.result: Integrating SMPs with SNPs improves demographic inference, especially in recent times, with as little as 2% of CG sites being sufficient for improvement. When epimutation rates are known, sharp demographic changes are accurately detected; when unknown, the shape is well inferred despite scaling issues.
results.evaluation: Figure 5A and 5B demonstrate demographic inference accuracy with varying proportions of methylation sites (2%, 10%, 20%), showing similar improvements across all proportions. Figure 5C and 5D show substantial improvements with limited sequence data (10 Mb). Supplementary file 1f provides quantitative RMSE values supporting these conclusions.

results.result: DMR data improves demographic inference when region-level epimutation rates are known, but provides no significant gain when rates are unknown, regardless of DMR length (1 kb or 150 bp).
results.evaluation: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2 demonstrate this differential performance based on whether epimutation rates are known. Supplementary file 1h provides RMSE values quantifying the accuracy differences. The result is consistent across different DMR lengths.

results.result: When both site and region-level epimutations occur at similar rates, inference accuracy depends on whether rates are known: unknown rates provide gains in recent times, while known rates lead to accuracy loss due to mislabeling of methylation region status. Ignoring either process decreases accuracy.
results.evaluation: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4 demonstrate these effects with clear mechanistic explanation (C69). The mislabeling occurs because methylated sites appear in unmethylated regions and vice versa when both processes operate at similar rates. Supplementary file 1i and j provide RMSE quantification.

results.result: In A. thaliana, DMRs cannot simply emerge from spontaneous site-level epimutations following Poisson processes. Instead, stochastic changes in region-level methylation require both site- and region-level processes, with epimutation independence requiring distances over 2 kb—larger than typical DMR sizes.
results.evaluation: Statistical tests reject binomial distribution of methylation sites for all 10 A. thaliana methylomes (C71). Figure 5—figure supplement 5 shows p-values <0.05 for distances up to 2,000 bp. The HMM yields DMR average length of 222 bp (C73, Figure 4B). The model-based comparison between simulations and observed data provides strong evidence for the necessity of both site- and region-level processes.

results.result: The epimutation model cannot fully describe observed methylation diversity in A. thaliana. LD between SMPs at distances <100 bp is much higher in data than simulations, non-independence spans regions larger than genealogy spans, and methylation likely violates Poisson process assumptions along the genome and in time.
results.evaluation: Figure 4C shows clear discrepancy between observed (red) and simulated (blue) LD patterns for SMPs at short distances. Figure 5—figure supplement 5 demonstrates non-independence beyond expected distances. These observations, combined with citations to recent functional studies, provide strong evidence for model violations.

results.result: Applying SMCm to A. thaliana German accessions reveals a post-Last Glacial Maximum bottleneck (5,000-10,000 generations ago) followed by expansion when using SMPs, which was not detected using SNPs alone. Inferred site epimutation rates are 10,000 times faster than DNA mutation rates, consistent with experimental measures.
results.evaluation: Figure 6 shows demographic inference results, with SNP-only analysis (purple) showing no clear post-LGM expansion, while SMP integration reveals bottleneck and expansion patterns (blue and green lines). However, the authors themselves express caution about result reliability due to model violations documented in C97-C99. The inferred epimutation rates (C85, Supplementary file 1k) match expected order of magnitude, but discrepancies with experimental measures are noted (C101). The biological interpretation requires additional validation given documented model violations.

results.result: Integrating epimutations slightly improves TMRCA inference accuracy when epimutation rates are known, but not when rates are unknown.
results.evaluation: Supplementary file 1g provides RMSE values quantifying TMRCA inference accuracy under different conditions. The improvement is modest and conditional on knowing epimutation rates, which is clearly documented.

results.result: The method accounts for the finite site problem at hyper-mutable markers and high effective population sizes, and LD comparisons across markers provide a useful diagnostic for model assumption violations.
results.evaluation: The finite site modeling is a design feature supported by theoretical citations (C91). Figure 4C and 4D demonstrate the utility of LD comparisons for detecting model violations, as evidenced by discrepancies between simulated and observed patterns.

results.result: Caution is warranted for conclusions about natural selection based on population epigenomic data due to model assumption violations. Current A. thaliana demographic results are limited by inability to simultaneously account for background selection, population structure, and molecular rate variation.
results.evaluation: This is a well-justified cautionary statement based on documented model violations (C97-C99) and known limitations in the field. Citations support that these evolutionary forces bias inference when not accounted for (C110). The statement appropriately tempers interpretation of results.

results.result: The consistency between SNP-based and methylation-based demographic inferences confirms that CG methylation sites are mainly heritable at the timescale of thousands of generations, and that fast ecological adaptation and stress responses are likely not prominent forces continuously reshaping CG methylation patterns.
results.evaluation: While the absence of conflicting demographic signals (Figure 6) provides some support, this inference is weakened by the documented model violations (C97-C99) and the uncertainty in the A. thaliana demographic results themselves. The conclusion about ecological adaptation and stress responses is speculative and based primarily on the absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence.

results.result: The approach provides tools to infer marker rates and distribution processes when evolutionary mechanisms are poorly understood, and can integrate well-characterized markers to improve SMC performance. Accurate marker annotation with inheritance and mutational information is advisable for optimal results.
results.evaluation: Table 1 demonstrates the ability to estimate unknown mutation rates (C115). Figure 5B and 5D show improved inference when rates are known (C116). These are practical recommendations well-supported by the simulation results throughout the manuscript.

results.result: An Ising model is suggested for modeling heterogeneous methylation processes, but preliminary work shows it generates non-homogeneous mutation processes violating current SMC assumptions. Continuous time Markov chains could address complexity from integrating multiple markers.
results.evaluation: These are speculative suggestions for future methodological development (C102, C130). The limitation of the Ising model approach is noted based on preliminary work and cited simulations (C103), but no concrete solution is demonstrated. These represent research directions rather than established results.

results.result: Technological advances in sequencing are improving genome quality and marker detection, which will enhance understanding of marker heritability and improve full genome approaches currently limited by nucleotide diversity. The framework is predicted to enable improved inference of biological traits, recombination rates, selection events, and represents the future direction of population genomics.
results.evaluation: These are primarily speculative predictions about future developments (C128, C131-C133) supported by citations to recent technological advances (C126, C127). While the technological trends are well-documented, the predicted improvements and applications remain to be demonstrated. These represent aspirational goals rather than established results.

results.result: The extended SMC framework can improve demographic inference in recent times, uncover hidden demographic events, infer hyper-mutable marker mutation rates, and integrate multiple heritable genomic markers to more accurately recover recent population size variation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the study 'extends existing sequentially Markovian coalescent approaches' and provides 'solid validation of their methods via simulation.' Reviewer 3 affirms 'there is no reason why the concept of this work is not conceptually sound,' endorsing the methodological framework. The core contribution is accepted by all reviewers.

results.result: Simulations demonstrate that including hyper-mutable markers correctly infers recent bottlenecks even when mutation rates are unknown, with as little as 0.1% hyper-mutable sites providing substantial improvement over SNP-only methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a 'major caveat' about 'strong dependence on knowing the epimutation rate,' noting that 'when the rate is not known' results may not look better. While simulations show improvement, Reviewer 2 questions whether 'results when the rates have to be estimated don't seem that much better than when focusing on SNPs alone,' creating uncertainty about practical performance.

results.result: The method can accurately recover site- and region-level epimutation rates except when very high (close to 10^-2), with average estimates within a factor of 10 even at extreme rates, and can recover mutation rates of other markers when SNP mutation rate is known.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 highlights that 'the estimated rates differ by a large amount from earlier published ones' in the real data analysis, questioning the reliability of rate estimation. While simulations show reasonable accuracy, the discrepancy with experimental measurements raises concerns about practical applicability.

results.result: Demographic inference with methylation data shows that when epimutation rates are known, bottlenecks can be accurately detected, and even 2% methylation coverage is sufficient for improvement; however, when rates are unknown, there is shape recovery but with scaling issues, and DMRs provide no significant gain without known rates.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 observes that 'when the epimutation rate is known, inferences do indeed look better; but this is not necessarily true when the rate is not known,' and notes 'a roughly similar pattern emerges in Supp. Figs. 4-7.' This conditional performance creates uncertainty about the method's practical utility when rates must be estimated.

results.result: Segregating single methylated polymorphisms (SMPs) satisfy SMC modeling assumptions with rapid LD decay, while DMRs are unsuitable because they are on average twice as large as genealogy spans (222 bp vs 137 bp), violating the assumption of homogeneous epimutation distribution.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'provide solid validation of their methods via simulation and analysis of empirical data,' implicitly accepting these findings about SMPs vs DMRs. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the distinction between individual CGs and regions, stating 'they do this both for individual CGs and small regions,' accepting the differential treatment.

results.result: Application to A. thaliana reveals that SNP-only analysis shows no strong post-LGM expansion, but including methylation data with known rates shows mild bottleneck and expansion, while estimating rates reveals a strong bottleneck 5,000-10,000 generations ago followed by expansion, potentially fitting post-LGM colonization of Europe.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the interpretation in Fig. 7 appears to hinge on whether the rates are known or estimated,' highlighting the sensitivity of conclusions to rate specification. The observation that 'estimated rates differ by a large amount from earlier published ones' raises questions about which demographic scenario is correct, creating uncertainty about the biological interpretation.

results.result: Model-based analysis provides strong evidence that DMRs cannot emerge from site-level Poisson processes alone, requiring both site- and region-level spontaneous methylation/demethylation events, with non-independence observed up to 2 kb, and methylation likely violating Poisson process assumptions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 accepts the 'analysis of empirical data in Arabidopsis thaliana' as solid validation. Reviewer 3 notes 'small regions containing multiple CGs can also be treated as genetic markers based on their cumulative methylation level,' implicitly accepting the region-level process. The mechanistic insights about epimutation processes are not challenged.

results.result: The epimutation model cannot fully describe observed diversity, caution is warranted about selection conclusions from epigenomic data due to model violations, and an Ising model is suggested for future development, though it would violate current SMC assumptions; nonetheless, focusing on SMPs in genic regions could meet assumptions reasonably well.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges the method 'may hold more promise as we get more and better epigenetic data, and in particular better knowledge of the epigenetic mutational process,' accepting that current understanding is incomplete. Reviewer 3's concern that 'it is not clear that CG methylation measurements are nearly as binary in other plants' aligns with recognition of model limitations.

results.result: Additional heritable markers like methylation may provide information on recent population history; CG methylation changes occur at rates 4-5 orders of magnitude faster than DNA mutations (10^-4 to 10^-3 per site per generation), are likely neutral genome-wide, and can be used as a molecular clock over years to decades.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 calls this 'an intriguing addition to infer population size history in the recent past.' Reviewer 3 states 'individual CGs in Arabidopsis tends to be either close to 100% methylated or close to 0%, and are inherited stably enough across generations that they can be treated as genetic markers,' endorsing the biological basis for using methylation.

results.result: Current A. thaliana demographic results are limited by inability to simultaneously account for background selection, population structure, and rate variation; however, the consistency between SNP and methylation-inferred demography confirms CG methylation heritability over thousands of generations and suggests fast ecological adaptation is not endlessly reshaping methylation patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges this is 'a foundation for further developments to explore when and where these methods will be best used,' accepting current limitations. Reviewer 2's concern about dependence on rates relates to methodology rather than challenging these specific biological interpretations.

results.result: The approach provides tools to study marker rates without experimental data when mechanisms are poorly understood, and can integrate markers to improve SMC when evolution is well understood; however, accurate marker annotation is advisable, gene body methylated genes are optimal but too sparse, and extra care is needed in other species due to tissue-specific methylation differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the concern that 'it is not clear that CG methylation measurements are nearly as binary in other plants and other eukaryotes as they are in Arabidopsis,' directly supporting the caution about generalization. Reviewer 1's statement that this is 'a foundation for further developments' accepts the current scope and limitations.

results.result: With new sequencing technology providing long accurate reads and better marker detection, there will be improved understanding of marker heritability, and adding genomic markers besides SNPs will improve full genome approaches; this work paves the way for improved inference of traits, recombination rates, selection events, and represents the future of population genomics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'given the increasing availability of such data, this work is a timely contribution.' Reviewer 3 concludes 'especially in the future as new sequencing technologies provide both base calling and methylating calling capabilities, using CG methylation in addition to SNPs could become a useful and feasible tool,' endorsing the future potential.

results.result: SNP-based inferences suffer from lack of statistical resolution for recent events like bottlenecks, especially when recombination rate exceeds mutation rate; the typical low mutation rate (10^-9 to 10^-8) places strong limitations on analyzing recent bottlenecks (up to ~10^4 generations), which are often not found or poorly estimated in timing and magnitude.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this as the motivation for the work. Reviewer 1 states the method provides 'better power to infer size history in the recent past,' accepting the limitation of SNPs. Reviewer 3 begins with 'a limitation in using SNPs to understand recent histories of genomes is their low mutation frequency,' explicitly endorsing this premise.
